front_blocks.md: Define **hydrogen bond**.

back_blocks.md: A **hydrogen bond** is the strongest type of intermolecular force, formed between a highly polarised O-H, N-H or F-H bond and a lone pair on an O, N or F atom in an adjacent molecule.

front_blocks.md: State the two conditions required for hydrogen bonding to occur between molecules.

back_blocks.md:
1. A molecule must contain a highly **electronegative** atom (**O, N or F**) with a **lone pair** of electrons.
2. A hydrogen atom must be covalently bonded directly to **O, N or F**, making the bond highly **polar**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Ice is denser than liquid water because the molecules in ice are more tightly packed.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Ice is **less dense** than liquid water. In ice, water molecules form a rigid open 3D hydrogen-bonded lattice with relatively long bond lengths, so the molecules are slightly further apart than in liquid water.

front_blocks.md: Why does water have a much higher enthalpy of vaporisation than expected from the trend in Group 16 hydrides?

back_blocks.md: The trend from H<sub>2</sub>S to H<sub>2</sub>Te suggests H<sub>2</sub>O should have an enthalpy of vaporisation of about 17 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. The actual value is almost three times larger because of the **additional energy needed to break hydrogen bonds** in water, which are absent in the other hydrides.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
NH<sub>3</sub> can form more hydrogen bonds per molecule than H<sub>2</sub>O.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

NH<sub>3</sub> can form up to **four** hydrogen bonds per molecule (one as acceptor via its lone pair on nitrogen, three as donors via N–H bonds) — the same maximum as H<sub>2</sub>O, not more. The statement is false because NH<sub>3</sub> cannot form **more** than H<sub>2</sub>O.

front_blocks.md: Why does water have a high surface tension?

back_blocks.md: Surface molecules are pulled **downwards** by hydrogen bonds with interior molecules. This compresses and tightens the surface layer, resisting external forces. Interior molecules are pulled in all directions so the net force is zero.

front_blocks.md: Define **electronegativity**.

back_blocks.md: **Electronegativity** is the ability of an atom to draw a pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent bond.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A covalent bond between two atoms of the same element is polar.

back_blocks.md: **False.** When two atoms have the same electronegativity, the bonding electrons are shared equally and the bond is **nonpolar**.

front_blocks.md: Define **dipole moment**.

front_blocks.md: What two factors must be considered when deciding whether a molecule with more than two atoms is polar overall?

back_blocks.md:
1. The **polarity of each bond** in the molecule.
2. The **arrangement** of those bonds — if individual dipole moments cancel each other out, the molecule is nonpolar overall.

CCl<sub>4</sub> is a polar molecule because it contains four polar C–Cl bonds.

back_blocks.md: **False.** Although CCl<sub>4</sub> contains four polar C–Cl bonds, the individual dipole moments cancel each other out due to the symmetrical tetrahedral arrangement, making CCl<sub>4</sub> a **nonpolar** molecule.

front_blocks.md: Explain why CH<sub>3</sub>Cl is a polar molecule but CCl<sub>4</sub> is not, even though both contain polar C–Cl bonds.

back_blocks.md: In CH<sub>3</sub>Cl the four polar bonds (three C–H and one C–Cl) do not cancel each other out, giving a **net dipole** towards the electronegative Cl atom. In CCl<sub>4</sub> the four identical C–Cl bond dipoles are arranged **symmetrically** and cancel each other out, so there is no overall dipole.

front_blocks.md: Define **van der Waals' forces**.

back_blocks.md: **Van der Waals' forces** are weak intermolecular forces between molecules. They include instantaneous dipole – induced dipole forces (London dispersion forces) and permanent dipole – permanent dipole forces.

front_blocks.md: What causes an instantaneous dipole to form in a non-polar molecule?

back_blocks.md: The electron charge cloud is constantly moving. At any moment it can be more concentrated on one side of the molecule than the other, creating a **temporary uneven distribution of charge** — an instantaneous dipole.

back_blocks.md: **Permanent dipole – permanent dipole forces** are the attractive intermolecular forces between the δ+ end of one polar molecule and the δ− end of a neighbouring polar molecule.

front_blocks.md: Propanone has a higher boiling point than butane, even though both molecules have the same number of electrons. Explain why.

back_blocks.md: Propanone is polar so it has **permanent dipole – permanent dipole forces** between its molecules. Butane is non-polar and only has weaker id–id forces. For molecules with the same number of electrons, pd–pd forces are **stronger** than id–id forces, so more energy is needed to separate propanone molecules.

front_blocks.md: Define **hydrogen bonding**.

back_blocks.md: **Hydrogen bonding** is a strong type of permanent dipole – permanent dipole intermolecular force. It forms between a δ+ H atom bonded to an O or N atom in one molecule and the lone pair on an O or N atom in a neighbouring molecule.

front_blocks.md: Why is the δ+ charge on H particularly large in molecules that form hydrogen bonds?

back_blocks.md: H is bonded to a highly electronegative O or N atom. The O or N atom draws nearly all the electron density from the O–H or N–H bond towards itself, leaving the H with a **large δ+** and the O/N with a **large δ−**.

front_blocks.md: Define **intramolecular forces**.

back_blocks.md: **Intramolecular forces** are forces **within** a molecule. The three types are ionic bonding, covalent bonding and metallic bonding.

front_blocks.md: What are the three types of intramolecular force and how does each form?

back_blocks.md:
1. **Ionic bonding** — electrostatic attraction between cations and anions formed by electron transfer.
2. **Covalent bonding** — formed when outer electrons of two atoms are shared.
3. **Metallic bonding** — electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons in a metal lattice.

3. **Metallic bonding** — electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons in a metal lattice.

front_blocks.md: Metallic bonding is described as an electrostatic attraction. What two species are attracted to each other?

back_blocks.md: In metallic bonding, **positively charged metal ions** (cations) are electrostatically attracted to the **delocalised electrons** that surround them in the metal lattice.
